This policy works alongside the Safe Administration of Medication Policy and Controlled Drugs Procedure
(governing staff-administered medication generally) and the Mental Capacity Act guidance (governing how
the capacity element of the assessment is conducted).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the removed exemption. A resident wishes to apply their own daily
moisturising cream, prescribed for a skin condition. Under this version, this now requires the same full
capacity and risk assessment as any other self-administered medication before it begins, whereas the
previous version allowed this without a full assessment given its topical, low-risk nature.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the topical exemption removed?** A review found a small number of topical medications
carried a meaningful risk, such as an interaction or an application error, that the exemption had not
accounted for; assessing every category consistently closes that gap. **How is the quarterly re-review
different from the annual review?** It is a lighter-touch check confirming nothing has changed since the
last full review, rather than repeating the complete assessment four times a year.

Training and competency

Registered managers complete self-administration assessment training, refreshed every two years,
updated to cover the removed topical exemption and the new quarterly re-review, and care staff receive an
overview of the arrangement as part of medication awareness training.

Monitoring and compliance

Active self-administration arrangements and both their annual and quarterly review dates are tracked on
the site's medication register, reviewed monthly by the registered manager.

Record keeping and retention

Capacity and risk assessments and their outcomes, including each quarterly re-review, are retained per
the Records Retention Schedule alongside the resident's wider care record.

Approval and review history

This policy was originally approved by the Chief Executive on 1 June 2025 and this version took effect 1
June 2026, superseding the earlier version.

capacity and risk assessment, and adds a new mandatory quarterly re-review for any resident
self-administering, in addition to the existing annual review.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group supports a resident who wishes to self-administer some
or all of their own medication. It applies to every site where a resident has capacity to make this choice.

Policy statement

Self-administration is supported wherever a resident has the capacity and genuine wish to manage their
own medication, since retaining this level of independence matters to a resident's own sense of control
over their daily life, balanced against a proportionate risk assessment.

Definitions

**Self-administration** a resident managing and taking their own medication themselves, rather than a
staff member administering it. **Capacity and risk assessment** the assessment completed before
self-administration begins for any self-administered medication, with no exempted category under this
version, reviewed annually with an additional quarterly re-review. **Topical medication** a cream, ointment
or patch applied to the skin, now assessed under the same standard as any other self-administered
medication.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** commissions the capacity and risk assessment before self-administration
begins, for every medication category, and schedules the new quarterly re-review. **The resident's GP or
a pharmacist** contributes clinical input to the assessment where relevant. **Care staff** monitor for any
sign that self-administration is no longer safe, reporting a concern to the registered manager rather than
deciding themselves to withdraw the arrangement.

1. Complete a capacity and risk assessment before self-administration begins for any medication,
including a topical medication; the previous exemption for topical medication from the full assessment has
been removed.

that self-administration is no longer safe, reporting a concern to the registered manager rather than
deciding themselves to withdraw the arrangement.

1. Complete a capacity and risk assessment before self-administration begins for any medication,
including a topical medication; the previous exemption for topical medication from the full assessment has
been removed.

2. Store self-administered medication in a lockable space in the resident's own room, with a spare key held
securely by staff for emergency access only.

3. Review the capacity and risk assessment annually, or sooner if a change in the resident's health or
circumstances suggests it may no longer be safe.

4. Complete an additional quarterly re-review for any resident currently self-administering, a new check
introduced in this version alongside the existing annual review.

5. Record what has been self-administered in the same records used for staff-administered medication, so
the full picture remains visible to a GP or pharmacist reviewing the resident's medication.

6. Withdraw a self-administration arrangement where the annual review, the quarterly re-review, or an
earlier concern, indicates it is no longer safe, discussing this sensitively with the resident first.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a resident's capacity appears to fluctuate rather than being consistently present, the registered
manager may agree a partial arrangement, for example self-administering a simple daily tablet while staff

A resident who has previously declined self-administration may request it at any time, and a fresh
assessment is offered rather than treating the earlier decision as final, since a resident's own confidence
and circumstances can change in either direction over time.

Supporting a resident with early memory difficulties

Where a resident has early-stage memory difficulties but otherwise retains relevant capacity,
self-administration may still be supported with a simple reminder system such as a labelled pill organiser
checked daily by staff, rather than assuming memory difficulty alone rules out self-administration entirely;
the quarterly re-review pays particular attention to this group.

What happens when a resident goes into hospital

Where a self-administering resident is admitted to hospital, their self-administration arrangement is
suspended for the duration of the admission and the capacity and risk assessment is revisited on their
return, since a hospital stay can itself change the resident's health status in a way that affects whether
self-administration remains appropriate; this revisit counts as that quarter's re-review where it falls within
the same window.

Closing note

Supporting self-administration where it is safe to do so is one concrete way this policy puts a resident's
own independence ahead of a purely risk-averse default, and the changes in this version exist to make
that safety judgement consistent across every medication category rather than only most of them.

Self-Administration of Medication Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group supports a resident who wishes to self-administer some
or all of their own medication. It applies to every site where a resident has capacity to make this choice.

Policy statement

Self-administration is supported wherever a resident has the capacity and genuine wish to manage their
own medication, since retaining this level of independence matters to a resident's own sense of control
over their daily life, balanced against a proportionate risk assessment.

Definitions

**Self-administration** a resident managing and taking their own medication themselves, rather than a
staff member administering it. **Capacity and risk assessment** the assessment completed before
self-administration begins, and reviewed annually thereafter. **Topical medication** a cream, ointment or
patch applied to the skin, treated under this version as a lower-risk category exempt from the full
assessment.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** commissions the capacity and risk assessment before self-administration
begins. **The resident's GP or a pharmacist** contributes clinical input to the assessment where relevant.
**Care staff** monitor for any sign that self-administration is no longer safe, reporting a concern to the
registered manager rather than deciding themselves to withdraw the arrangement.

1. Complete a capacity and risk assessment before self-administration begins for any medication other
than a topical medication, which may be self-administered without the full assessment under this version.

2. Store self-administered medication in a lockable space in the resident's own room, with a spare key held
securely by staff for emergency access only.

3. Review the capacity and risk assessment annually, or sooner if a change in the resident's health or
circumstances suggests it may no longer be safe.

circumstances suggests it may no longer be safe.

4. Record what has been self-administered in the same records used for staff-administered medication, so
the full picture remains visible to a GP or pharmacist reviewing the resident's medication.

5. Withdraw a self-administration arrangement where the annual review, or an earlier concern, indicates it

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a resident's capacity appears to fluctuate rather than being consistently present, the registered
manager may agree a partial arrangement, for example self-administering a simple daily tablet while staff
continue to administer a more complex regimen, rather than an all-or-nothing decision.

Local and regional variations

Willow Bank's community-visiting model means a self-administering resident's supply is checked at each
scheduled visit rather than daily, given the lower frequency of staff presence compared with a residential
site.

What happens when a resident goes into hospital

Where a self-administering resident is admitted to hospital, their self-administration arrangement is
suspended for the duration of the admission and the capacity and risk assessment is revisited on their
return, since a hospital stay can itself change the resident's health status in a way that affects whether
self-administration remains appropriate.

Involving the resident's family appropriately

A resident's family is told, with the resident's consent, that a self-administration arrangement is in place,
since a family member unaware of the arrangement has occasionally raised a well-intentioned but
mistaken concern that staff were failing to administer medication that the resident was in fact managing
themselves.

Interaction with a changing prescription

Where a resident's prescription changes, for example a new medication is added or a dose is altered, the
self-administration arrangement is reviewed at that point rather than only at the next scheduled annual
review, since a prescription change is exactly the kind of event that can affect whether continued
self-administration remains straightforward and safe for the resident to manage.

Closing note

Supporting self-administration where it is safe to do so is one concrete way this policy puts a resident's
own independence ahead of a purely risk-averse default, without losing sight of the safety the assessment
exists to protect.
